clinicalPearls: Malnutrition affects roughly 30-50% of hospitalized patients, with the exact prevalence varying by clinical setting, underlying diagnosis, and the diagnostic criteria applied (Harrison 22e p.2615).

The 2019 GLIM (Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition) consensus requires at least one phenotypic criterion (nonvolitional weight loss, low BMI, or reduced muscle mass) PLUS at least one etiologic criterion (reduced food intake/assimilation, or disease burden/inflammation) to diagnose malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.2616).

Severity grading in GLIM is determined by the phenotypic criterion: moderate (stage 1) malnutrition is 5-10% weight loss within 6 months (or 10-20% beyond 6 months), and severe (stage 2) is >10% within 6 months (or >20% beyond) (Harrison 22e p.2616).

Patients at any BMI can be malnourished; overweight or obese individuals may have sarcopenic obesity from muscle loss, and conversely being underweight does not by itself equal malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.2617).

Handgrip strength is among the more clinically useful functional measures because it is easy to perform and helps identify which patients are most likely to benefit from individualized nutritional support (Harrison 22e p.2617).
Patients with apparently adequate oral intake may still be at risk of malnutrition when chronic gastrointestinal disease compromises nutrient assimilation or absorption (Harrison 22e p.2617).
A 5-10% loss of body weight over 6 months is clinically relevant, while >10% loss over the same period is considered severe (Harrison 22e p.2617).

Albumin and prealbumin are negative acute-phase reactants and fall with injury, disease, or inflammation; they have poor sensitivity and specificity for malnutrition, though they retain value for predicting clinical outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.2617-2618).

C-reactive protein is a positive acute-phase reactant useful for confirming inflammation, with the chapter noting supportive thresholds of mild 3.0-9.9 mg/L, moderate 10-50 mg/L, and severe >50 mg/L (Harrison 22e p.2616).

Calf circumference is a practical, valid estimate of skeletal muscle mass that requires less training than mid-upper arm circumference, with ethnicity-specific reference ranges that should be adjusted for BMI extremes (Harrison 22e p.2618).
When inflammation is severe, nutrition care tends to be supportive only; at low-to-moderate inflammation, nutrition care may be therapeutic and improve clinical outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.2615-2616).
Calf circumference, BMI, and other GLIM parameters make malnutrition diagnosis feasible even in the outpatient/ambulatory setting where dietitian access may be limited (Harrison 22e p.2617).
harrison.pathophysiology: Malnutrition arises from an imbalance between nutrient intake/assimilation and metabolic demand, and acute or chronic inflammation is now recognized as central to its pathophysiology. Inflammatory mediators raise resting energy expenditure, promote anabolic resistance and muscle catabolism, and cause anorexia that further reduces intake. Severe acute inflammation (e.g., critical illness, sepsis, burns, trauma, closed head injury) may be superimposed on a mild-to-moderate chronic inflammatory state (e.g., malignancy, COPD, congestive heart failure, chronic renal disease, chronic GI disease). The resulting deficits impair wound healing, immune function, and organ function. Because albumin and prealbumin behave as negative acute-phase reactants, the inflammatory milieu also distorts these traditional nutrition biomarkers (Harrison 22e pp.2615-2617).
additionalDifferentials: Sarcopenia (progressive generalized loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength; screened with SARC-F)
Cachexia of chronic disease (malignancy, organ failure)
Dehydration / fluid shifts mimicking weight change
nonInfectiousMimics: Edema or fluid overload masking true weight loss (dry weight estimation may be needed)
Hypoalbuminemia from systemic inflammation, hepatic or renal insufficiency, protein-losing enteropathy, or corticosteroid use rather than nutrition itself
Low BUN/creatinine from renal or hepatic disease falsely suggesting reduced muscle mass
Hypocholesterolemia related to acute illness rather than malnutrition per se
additionalInvestigations: Validated risk-screening tools: Malnutrition Screening Tool, Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), Nutritional Risk Screening 2002, Mini Nutritional Assessment, Subjective Global Assessment
Anthropometrics: serial body weight (without shoes/heavy garments), BMI, calf circumference, mid-upper arm circumference; height estimated by arm span or knee-height caliper when needed
Body composition: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA, portable), dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), air displacement plethysmography, and opportunistic CT/MRI muscle measurement
Laboratory: complete blood count with differential (screen for iron, B12, folate, vitamin C deficiencies), C-reactive protein for inflammation, specific micronutrient levels
Indirect calorimetry for resting energy expenditure; 24-h urine urea nitrogen and nitrogen balance to gauge catabolism and protein adequacy (normal renal/hepatic function required)
Functional tests: handgrip strength, Sit-to-Stand test, 6-Meter Walk Test, Clinical Frailty Scale, SARC-F
Nutrition-focused physical examination for edema, subcutaneous fat and muscle loss; diet history including oral supplements, enteral and parenteral intake
redFlags: Nonvolitional weight loss >10% within 6 months (or >20% beyond 6 months) indicating severe malnutrition
BMI <18.5 kg/m2 in adults <70 years (or <20 if >=70 years) indicating severe malnutrition by GLIM
Severe acute inflammatory state with negative nitrogen balance and elevated resting energy expenditure
Low handgrip strength predicting poorer clinical outcomes
Hypocholesterolemia (<120 mg/dL) developing during hospitalization, linked to worse outcomes
Reduced food intake/assimilation (<=50% of energy requirement for >1 week, any reduction >2 weeks, or chronic GI condition impairing absorption)
harrison.prognosis: Malnutrition is associated with poor wound healing, compromised immunity, and impaired organ function, leading to longer hospital stays, more readmissions, higher mortality, and increased health care costs. Severe inflammation may limit nutritional interventions to a supportive rather than therapeutic role, and the associated malnutrition can diminish the effectiveness of medical therapies. Robust evidence indicates that a multipronged approach to malnutrition intervention reduces mortality and holds promise for improving quality of life, so timely diagnosis and treatment are important (Harrison 22e pp.2615, 2618).
pitfalls: Relying on albumin or prealbumin to diagnose malnutrition or judge response to nutrition therapy; they reflect inflammation, hepatic/renal status, hydration, and other factors and have poor specificity (Harrison 22e pp.2617-2618).
Assuming a normal or high BMI excludes malnutrition; sarcopenic obesity and muscle loss can occur at any BMI (Harrison 22e p.2617).
Overlooking edema, which can mask true weight loss unless dry weight is estimated (Harrison 22e p.2617).

Using BUN/creatinine, total lymphocyte count, cholesterol, creatinine-height index, cytokines, ECG, recall-antigen skin testing, or urine 3-methylhistidine as malnutrition indicators; the chapter lists these as NOT recommended for diagnosis (Harrison 22e pp.2618-2619).
Comparing malnutrition prevalence across studies without accounting for differences between diagnostic tools, which yield incomparable rates (Harrison 22e p.2616).
Failing to recognize prolonged pre-admission decreases in intake when an acute event is superimposed on chronic disease (Harrison 22e p.2617).
harrison.severityClassification: GLIM severity grading by phenotypic criteria. Stage 1 (moderate): weight loss 5-10% within 6 months or 10-20% beyond 6 months; BMI <20 (<70 years) or <22 (>=70 years); mild-to-moderate muscle mass deficit. Stage 2 (severe): weight loss >10% within 6 months or >20% beyond 6 months; BMI <18.5 (<70 years) or <20 (>=70 years); severe muscle mass deficit. WHO/NIH BMI categories: <18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 desirable, 25.0-29.9 overweight, >=30 obese (Harrison 22e pp.2616-2617).
management: Screen with a validated tool such as the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool and diagnose using GLIM phenotypic and aetiologic criteria
Deliver an individualised plan prioritising the oral route with dietary counselling, food fortification and oral nutritional supplements
Provide enteral tube feeding when oral intake is inadequate and the gut functions, reserving parenteral nutrition for an unusable gastrointestinal tract
Identify patients at risk of refeeding syndrome, reintroduce nutrition cautiously with thiamine and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium
Correct micronutrient and vitamin deficiencies including iron, vitamin B12, folate, vitamin C and vitamin D
Treat the underlying disease and inflammatory burden, recognising that severe inflammation limits the response to nutritional support
Monitor weight, dietary intake, biochemistry and functional measures such as handgrip strength to gauge response
Coordinate dietitian-led multidisciplinary care, involving speech and language therapy where dysphagia contributes
